new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked the copy we hold (16 pp., pages stored out of order: PDF p. 8 = printed p. 83) and the page render. The quoted passage is on printed p. 83 exactly as reported: "Besides these segmental phonemes there are three lexically contrastive supra-segmental phonemes in these languages: vowel tone--or vowel stress--/´/ in each language; vowel length /:/ written as the second vowel of geminate sequences: /ii/, /ee/, /aa/, /oo/ and /uu/ in Ekagi and Wodani, but not in Moni; vowel nasalization /ⁿ/ in Wodani and Moni, but not in Ekagi." and, lower on the same page, "Thus while in all three languages /d/ may be manifested by an implosive (d') in utterance-initial stressed syllable, only in Wodani a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only published phonological description states that Wolani (Wodani) has a lexically contrastive prosodic feature marked /´/ on a vowel, which the authors call 'vowel tone--or vowel stress' without deciding between the two; no placement rule is given, so accent position must be treated as lexically specified (unpredictable) from this source. Voorhoeve 1975: 408, summarising this paper, calls the language tonal. The paper's wordlist (Appendix A) does not mark the accent, so no distribution can be inferred from it.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the source gives no rule at all, only the existence of the lexical contrast.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (lexically contrastive on vowels of open (C)V / (C)VV syllables); 'utterance-initial stressed syllable' is mentioned only as the environment for implosive [d]. Data from the Upper Mbiyandoga dialect (WO-umb), with Mid-Kemandoga (mk) noted as sharing the same system apart from /s/. Note the tone/stress equivocation: a reading of 'tone language with a stress statement' is equally defensible.
new_statements.identity_note: The source calls the language Wodani (also 'Wodaa'); Voorhoeve 1975 and Glottolog equate Wodani = Wolani = Woda [wod], wola1243. Data are from the Upper Mbiyandoga dialect (WO-umb) with Mid-Kemandoga (WO-mk) noted as identical apart from /s/; the statement is made jointly for Ekagi, Wodani and Moni ('in each language'). The printed byline reads 'Gordon F. Larson and Mildred O. Larson' (Glottolog's record has 'Milfred O.').

sources.note: p. 408 (2.6.2.2.10.1.2 Wodani): three dialects (upper/lower Mbiyandoga, mid-Kemandoga); sources Le Roux 1950 (short wordlist) and Larson & Larson 1972 ('contains only phonological data'); gives the sound system and ends 'Vowel nasalization is distinctive; the language is tonal.' Second-hand summary of Larson & Larson; nothing on stress placement.
